Steve Jobs
A Life of Vision, Innovation, and Relentless Pursuit of Excellence
Early Life and Adoption
Steve Paul Jobs was born on February 24, 1955, in San Francisco, California. He was
given up for adoption at birth by his biological parents, Joanne Schieble and Abdulfattah
Jandali, a Syrian graduate student. He was adopted by Paul and Clara Jobs, a
working-class couple from Mountain View, California. Paul Jobs was a machinist and
carpenter who taught young Steve how to work with his hands, instilling in him an early
appreciation for craftsmanship and attention to detail. Clara Jobs was an accountant who
taught Steve to read before he started school. From a very young age, Steve showed a
deep curiosity about how things worked, often taking apart and reassembling electronics in
the family garage.
Childhood and Education
Growing up in the heart of what would later become Silicon Valley, Steve Jobs was
surrounded by engineers and electronics hobbyists. He attended Homestead High School
in Cupertino, California, where he met Steve Wozniak, who would later become his partner
in founding Apple. Jobs was an intelligent but restless student who struggled with formal
education. After graduating high school in 1972, he enrolled at Reed College in Portland,
Oregon, but dropped out after just one semester, feeling guilty about the financial burden
his tuition placed on his working-class adoptive parents. However, he continued to attend
classes that interested him, most notably a calligraphy course that would later influence the
beautiful typography of the Macintosh computer. This decision to follow his curiosity rather
than a formal curriculum would define his approach to life and business for decades to
come.
The Founding of Apple
In 1976, at the age of 21, Steve Jobs co-founded Apple Computer Company with Steve
Wozniak and Ronald Wayne in the Jobs family garage. Wozniak had built a revolutionary
personal computer circuit board, and Jobs saw its commercial potential. Jobs convinced
Wozniak to partner with him to sell the machine. The Apple I sold for $666.66 and
established the company as a serious player in the emerging personal computer market.
The Apple II, released in 1977, was a massive commercial success and is credited with

kickstarting the personal computer revolution. It was one of the first highly successful
mass-produced microcomputers. The company grew rapidly, and on December 12, 1980,
Apple went public in one of the most successful IPOs in history, creating more millionaires
overnight than any company up to that point.
The Macintosh and Departure from Apple
In 1984, Apple launched the Macintosh, the first commercially successful personal
computer to feature a graphical user interface and a mouse. The launch was accompanied
by a now-legendary Super Bowl advertisement directed by Ridley Scott, portraying Apple
as a liberator fighting against conformity. The Macintosh was a revolutionary product, but
its high price and limited software led to disappointing sales. Internal power struggles
between Jobs and then-CEO John Sculley, whom Jobs had personally recruited from
Pepsi, resulted in the Apple board siding with Sculley. In 1985, Jobs was stripped of his
management responsibilities and subsequently resigned from Apple, the company he had
co-founded. He sold all but one of his Apple shares and walked away from the company
that was his life's work.
NeXT and Pixar
After leaving Apple, Jobs founded NeXT Inc. in 1985, a computer platform development
company that manufactured workstation computers aimed at the higher education and
business markets. Although NeXT computers were technically advanced and influential in
many ways, they were too expensive for mainstream adoption. However, the NeXT
operating system and software would later become the foundation for Apple's Mac OS X.
During this period, Jobs also acquired the computer graphics division of Lucasfilm from
George Lucas in 1986 for $10 million. He renamed it Pixar Animation Studios. Under his
leadership and with substantial personal investment, Pixar produced groundbreaking
computer-animated films. The release of Toy Story in 1995, the world's first fully
computer-animated feature film, was a massive critical and commercial success. Pixar's
IPO on November 29, 1995, made Jobs a billionaire. Disney later acquired Pixar in 2006
for $7.4 billion, making Jobs Disney's largest individual shareholder.
Return to Apple
In 1996, Apple, struggling financially and without a modern operating system, acquired
NeXT for approximately $429 million, bringing Jobs back to the company he had founded.
He initially served as an advisor before being named interim CEO in 1997. He quickly
moved to simplify Apple's product line, cutting it from 350 products to just 10. He

renegotiated Apple's deal with Microsoft, securing a $150 million investment that helped
stabilize the company. His return sparked a dramatic turnaround. In 1998, Apple
introduced the iMac, a colorful all-in-one computer that became a design icon and restored
Apple's image as an innovative company. Jobs officially became CEO in 2000, dropping
the interim title. He led Apple to become one of the most valuable companies in the world
over the next decade.
The iPod, iTunes, and the Digital Revolution
In 2001, Apple released the iPod, a portable music player that could hold one thousand
songs in your pocket, as Jobs famously proclaimed. Combined with the iTunes Music
Store, launched in 2003, Apple revolutionized the music industry. For the first time,
consumers could legally purchase individual songs online for 99 cents. Within a year,
Apple had sold over 70 million songs. The iPod became Apple's best-selling product for
several years and introduced millions of people to Apple products who had previously used
Windows PCs. It was the beginning of Apple's transformation from a computer company
into a consumer electronics powerhouse. By 2007, the iPod commanded 73.8 percent of
the United States music player market.
The iPhone
On January 9, 2007, Steve Jobs took to the stage at the Macworld Conference and Expo in
San Francisco and announced that Apple would be releasing a phone that was an iPod, a
phone, and an internet communicator all in one device. The iPhone fundamentally changed
the smartphone industry and the way people interact with technology. It introduced the
concept of a large multi-touch screen, eliminating the need for a physical keyboard. The
device ran a full version of the internet, not a stripped-down mobile version. It popularized
the concept of mobile apps through the App Store, launched in 2008, which created an
entirely new economy. The iPhone became the most successful product in consumer
electronics history and is still Apple's primary revenue driver. It transformed industries from
photography to navigation, banking, and social media.
The iPad and Later Years
In 2010, Jobs introduced the iPad, a tablet computer that he described as more intimate
than a laptop and more capable than a smartphone. Critics initially dismissed it as a large
iPhone, but consumers embraced it enthusiastically. The iPad sold over 300,000 units on
its first day and over 3 million in its first 80 days. It created an entirely new product category
and transformed how people consume media, play games, and do work. By this time,

however, Jobs health had been declining. He had been diagnosed with a rare form of
pancreatic cancer in 2003 and had undergone a liver transplant in 2009. Despite his
declining health, Jobs continued to drive Apple's product development with characteristic
intensity. He took several medical leaves of absence but remained deeply involved in the
company's direction.
Leadership Style and Philosophy
Steve Jobs was known for his demanding, often difficult management style. He pushed his
teams relentlessly, famously telling engineers that their work was a consequence of their
choices, not their limitations. He had an extraordinary ability to focus on what mattered
most and to simplify complex problems. His famous reality distortion field, a term coined by
Apple employees, described his ability to convince people that the impossible was
achievable. He believed deeply in the intersection of technology and liberal arts, insisting
that Apple products must be both technically excellent and beautifully designed. He had an
obsessive attention to detail that extended even to parts of products that customers would
never see. He believed that great design was not just about aesthetics but about function
and simplicity. His product presentations, known as Stevenotes, became legendary events
that set the standard for how technology companies launch products.
Personal Life
Steve Jobs's personal life was as complex as his professional one. He had a daughter,
Lisa Brennan-Jobs, from a relationship with Chrisann Brennan, whom he initially denied
paternity of despite DNA tests. He later reconciled with Lisa and she became part of his
life. In 1991, he married Laurene Powell in a Buddhist ceremony. Together they had three
children: Reed, Erin, and Eve. Jobs was deeply influenced by Zen Buddhism, which
shaped his minimalist aesthetic sensibilities and his approach to focus and clarity. He was
known to be a vegetarian for much of his life, though he cycled through various extreme
dietary practices. He was intensely private about his personal life and his health struggles.
Illness and Death
Steve Jobs was diagnosed with a rare form of pancreatic cancer called an islet cell
neuroendocrine tumor in October 2003. He delayed surgery for nine months, instead trying
alternative treatments including a special diet and spiritual therapies, a decision he later
said he regretted. He underwent surgery in 2004 and received a liver transplant in
Memphis, Tennessee in April 2009. On August 24, 2011, Jobs resigned as CEO of Apple,
saying he could no longer meet the duties and expectations that came with the role. He

recommended Tim Cook as his successor. Steve Jobs died on October 5, 2011, at the age
of 56, at his home in Palo Alto, California, surrounded by his family. The cause of death
was complications from pancreatic cancer. His death was mourned around the world, with
tributes pouring in from world leaders, artists, technologists, and millions of ordinary people
whose lives had been touched by his products.
Legacy
Steve Jobs left behind a legacy that is difficult to overstate. Under his leadership, Apple
became the most valuable company in the world and introduced products that
fundamentally changed how humanity communicates, consumes entertainment, and
interacts with information. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest business
executives and product visionaries in history. His insistence on combining technology with
great design influenced an entire generation of entrepreneurs and product designers. The
iPhone alone transformed multiple industries and created the modern mobile economy. His
story of being adopted, dropping out of college, being fired from his own company, and
returning to lead it to unprecedented success has inspired countless people around the
world. Apple's market capitalization surpassed one trillion dollars in 2018, seven years
after his death, a testament to the culture and direction he established. Steve Jobs proved
that one person with a clear vision and relentless determination can truly change the world.
